extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in mathematics and computer science learning mathematical writing and copy editing (e.g., participants in a CS/math writing class)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for clear, accurate, and effective mathematical/technical writing and copy-editing, covering semantics, syntax, symbols, style, organization, punctuation, and proof exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, coherence, accuracy, and concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Good writing should strive to be clear, coherent, accurate, and concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General injunction repeated: answer more questions than you raise; remove needless words; prefer clarity over ornament. Quote: Pascal — making something shorter takes effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize material (Do organize)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize material so the reader can recognize structure and follow the exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organization is more than linear order; weave branches and alternative threads together. Inspect examples of progressively complex organization (thesaurus, encyclopedia, textbook). The instructor spends most writing time on organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distract the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid constructions and stylistic choices that distract the reader from the ideas being communicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distracting elements include awkward grammar, unnecessary punctuation conventions, gratuitous novelty in notation, or stylistic quirks that draw attention away from content. (Exception: purposely distract to jar readers.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer short sentences; avoid long, semicolon-laden sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, replace one long sentence with two short ones; semicolons slow pace and should be rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a semicolon only when clauses have a very close relationship; often a period is better. 'Out with the semicolons, in with the periods.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep subject and verb in proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid separating the subject and verb with many intervening words; such separations make sentences harder to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reorder or shorten phrases so the reader can parse subject-verb-object quickly; example: move subject near verb to improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delete unnecessary filler words and phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove superfluous words that do not add meaning (e.g., 'out', 'he has heard', 'the reason ... is that').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace indirect constructions ('the reason for removing the spaces from the list is that ...') with direct ones ('We remove the spaces because ...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conversational idioms in technical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use informal, conversational phrases (e.g., 'Anyway', 'pretty straightforward', 'again iterate through') in formal technical prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such idioms sound awkward in research/technical papers and detract from precision and tone; rewrite more smoothly and precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive voice and unnecessary 'we'; prefer subject-verb-object or imperative
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce passive constructions and use of 'we' when they add an irrelevant dimension; consider imperative or indicative styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Multiply each b.z by this factor' instead of passive 'Each of the b.z's are then multiplied by this factor.' Using 'we' is not a crime but often avoidable; 'Replace x by 7 throughout.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use commas correctly for parenthetical insertions
rubrics_metrics.description: If using commas to insert a parenthetical note, place commas on both sides of the insertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '... this node, b, is thus ...' — both sides must have commas around the parenthetical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague modifiers and colloquial intensifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'really', 'very', 'just', or vague phrases make technical writing imprecise; prefer concrete criteria or explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'saving the computation for the place where it is really needed' with a specific condition like 'saving the computation for those vertices where the additional work contributes more to the visual quality.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Place 'only' adjacent to what it modifies
rubrics_metrics.description: Misplaced 'only' changes the meaning of sentences; its position determines scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by inserting 'only' in each position of 'I hit him in the eye yesterday' producing eight distinct readings. Use 'Here we calculate the position of only two vertices' vs 'Here we only calculate the position of two vertices.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse/repetition of small words ('this', 'then', 'just')
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent repetition of small words reduces readability and style quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud helps spot over-use; remove or vary repeated words to improve flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate noise-phrases when they add nothing ('in the context of', etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases that can be deleted without loss of meaning should be removed unless they serve to re-anchor the topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes repetition of a phrase early in a piece can make a later repetition useful to reorient the reader; judge case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise word choice; maintain semantic distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confuse words with different meanings (e.g., 'imply' vs 'infer', 'disinterested' vs 'uninterested', 'alternately' vs 'alternatively').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confusing such words loses valuable distinctions; a list of commonly conflated pairs is provided to watch for errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer numerals to words when ambiguity arises (symbols & numerals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid ambiguity between the word 'one' as numeral vs pronoun by using the numeral '1' when you mean the numeral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'What are we to do when x is one?' — use 'x is 1' if numeral intended. Use numerals to avoid misreading in mathematical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate quotations logically (placement of quotation marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place quotation marks in a logically clear position rather than blindly following typographic conventions that may mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paul urges logical placement of quotes every time; typographic conventions (e.g., Chicago) may place punctuation awkwardly relative to logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect grammar/case as a form of logical organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammar (case, tense, agreement) conveys logical information; correct grammatical forms aid clarity of thought and communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'I don't know him' vs 'I don't know he.' Use 'who' vs 'whom' correctly according to grammatical function to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-of-sentence preposition rule is flexible; avoid awkward constructs
rubrics_metrics.description: The admonition against ending sentences with prepositions is overly reactionary; such endings are often acceptable unless they produce an awkward double-preposition structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where final prepositions are natural: 'Palo Alto is a good place to live in.' Avoid sentences that already accommodate a preposition in the middle and then add another at the end awkwardly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid echoing unusual words across unrelated passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not repeat unusual words in unrelated passages, as it creates spurious associations in the reader's mind and may cause typist issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Echoing can produce unwarranted connections; paraphrase or vary vocabulary for clarity and to avoid monotony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'that' judiciously for clarity in complex sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitting 'that' can improve sentences, but in complicated technical sentences it can be needed to preserve syntactic clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'He said he was going' may be better than 'He said that he was going' in simple cases; retain 'that' when it aids parsing in complex sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'then' appropriately in conditionals (context-sensitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: In everyday language 'then' is often omitted in 'if ... then ...' constructions, but in mathematical contexts 'then' can aid comprehension and parsing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For speed and parsing in technical writing, well-placed 'then's can make statements clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid proof by contradiction when a direct proof is available
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer direct proofs for exposition because proofs by contradiction are often circuitous and harder for readers to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contradiction while solving, but rewrite for exposition when a direct argument is available (e.g., linear independence proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be conservative with exclamation points and expressive punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclamation points should be used only for actual exclamations or interjections; avoid casual overuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities discourage gratuitous exclamation points; a humorous workaround is placing it in parentheses for surprise — '(!)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be pragmatic about split infinitives
rubrics_metrics.description: The blanket rule to avoid split infinitives is unwise; splitting can provide useful emphasis and may sound forced if avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide by ear and rhetorical effect rather than strict rule-following.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and accept technical jargon where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical terms sometimes serve as verbs or specialized usages in a discipline (e.g., 'reference'/'de-reference' in CS); adjust style expectations accordingly for the intended audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing for a technical audience, accept discipline-specific usages; when writing for a general audience, avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincident punctuation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When two punctuation marks would coincide (e.g., two commas, comma+period), follow conventional simplifications (write one comma; prefer the period when comma+period coincide).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coincident punctuation is not inherently a sign of bad construction; write only the required mark(s) per convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous modifier scope (e.g., 'fine' modifying books vs collectors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure modifiers unambiguously attach to the intended noun to prevent misreading (e.g., 'fine book collectors' vs 'collectors of fine books').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rephrase to make modification explicit when ambiguity arises.
